newsitem.title: USA: CBOT calls delivery terms "core issue" for members.
newsitem.headline: CBOT calls delivery terms "core issue" for members.

text.p: A leader of the Chicago Board of Trade said Thursday that the exchange's proposal to change delivery terms of its corn and soybean contracts was a "core issue" that the CBOT would fight for in court if necessary.
"The delivery terms are a core issue for the membership of the exchange," Bill Evans, chairman of the CBOT's grain delivery task force, told Reuters.

"And the bigger issue is whether the exchange has the right to make these business-related decisions," added Evans, a CBOT trader with Iowa Grain Co. "One option would be to let a judge decide all this."
Evans, flanked by a half-dozen economics professors, traders and grain experts hired by the CBOT, appeared before a rare public hearing held by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

He defended CBOT's controversial proposal to jettison the port of Toledo as a delivery point for the exchange's corn and soybean contracts and replace it with warehouse facilities along the northern Illinois River.

The recommendation has been vigorously opposed by Ohio politicians, farm groups and some grain exporters. They claim Toledo helps prevent price manipulation and serves grain buyers in the eastern corn belt of the United States.

"We simply haven't seen a better deal," Evans said in an interview after speaking to the five-member CFTC. "This meets the criteria of the Commodity Exchange Act. It's not about politics or regional interests."
The CFTC is accepting public comments on the exchange's proposal until June 16, and has said it will act on the issue as swiftly as possible.

CFTC chair Brooksley Born said at the hearing that the commission was required by law to determine whether the delivery terms proposed by the CBOT would tend to prevent or diminish price manipulation.
The agency will also consider the public interest to be protected by antitrust laws, she said.
"In applying these legal standards, the commission is not free to substitute its business judgment for that of the CBOT," Born said in a statement.

"The unprecedented number of comments received by the commission underscores the significant impact on the CBOT's actions on those who are engaged in business in the underlying cash markets and who may or may not be members of the exchange or trade on it," she added, referring to the more than 500 letters sent to the CFTC since earlier this spring.
During the four-hour hearing, Born and the other CFTC commissioners gave no hint of how they might ultimately rule on the proposal.

The commissioners queried the CBOT representatives on several issues, including what calculations were used to determine market concentration and what procedure would be used to make any further modifications to delivery terms should the proposal be adopted in its current form.
"Does the CBOT have no reservations, based on the hundreds of comments received (by the CFTC)?" asked Born at one point during the hearing.

Evans responded by saying the proposal was fashioned to best serve the interests of all market players. "This isn't a popularity contest," he said. "We're not mad at Toledo and we're not out to get the people of Toledo."
